stem: What is price analysis?

options.text: Examining a price without evaluating its separate cost elements and profit
options.why: That is the FAR definition.

options.text: Auditing the contractor's accounting records to verify its labor costs
options.why: That is audit work, often by DCAA.

options.text: Evaluating each cost element and the proposed profit to build up a price
options.why: That is cost analysis.

options.text: Comparing the technical proposals of the offerors against the criteria
options.why: That is technical evaluation.

stem: Which two price analysis techniques does the FAR treat as preferred?

options.text: Comparing competing prices, and comparing with prior prices for the same or similar items
options.why: These two come first in the FAR's list.

options.text: Comparing with the IGCE, and asking the contractor to explain how it built its price
options.why: These are useful but not the preferred techniques.

options.text: Parametric estimates and rough yardsticks such as dollars per pound
options.why: Useful as checks, not the preferred techniques.

options.text: Reviewing the contractor's labor rates, overhead and profit
options.why: That is cost analysis.

stem: Adequate price competition exists when:

options.text: Two or more responsible offerors compete independently with offers that meet the need
options.why: Those are the core conditions in FAR 15.403-2(c)(1), together with award on best value where price is a substantial factor and no finding that the winning price is unreasonable.

options.text: A single offer comes in below the IGCE after the solicitation was posted to everyone
options.why: One offer is not competition.

options.text: Three related companies submit quotes that are close to each other
options.why: Offerors must compete independently.

options.text: The incumbent and one other firm both submit offers, even if the firms are related
options.why: Incumbency has nothing to do with it.

stem: You compare a quote with a price paid 14 months ago for the same item. What should you adjust for?

options.text: Time (inflation), quantity and differences in terms
options.why: Prior prices are only comparable after adjusting for what changed.

options.text: Nothing; the same item means the same price
options.why: Markets and quantities change.

options.text: Only shipping costs, since the item is the same
options.why: Shipping is one difference, not the only one.

options.text: The contractor's profit margin at the time of the earlier sale
options.why: Price analysis does not break out profit.

stem: What is unbalanced pricing?

options.text: Line items priced far too high or too low, even if the total looks fine
options.why: Unbalanced pricing hides risk inside line items.

options.text: Any total price above the IGCE by more than ten percent
options.why: A high total is not the same as unbalanced line items.

options.text: A price below the contractor's cost, offered to win the contract
options.why: That is a buy-in risk, a different issue.

options.text: An offer received late that changes its prices after the others
options.why: Lateness is unrelated.

stem: On a simplified buy you receive only one quote. What does the contracting officer do?

options.text: Still find the price fair and reasonable using other evidence, and document it
options.why: A single quote can be reasonable when other evidence supports it.

options.text: Cancel the buy and resolicit to get at least three quotes
options.why: One quote does not require cancellation.

options.text: Require certified cost or pricing data from the single vendor
options.why: Certified data are never required at or below the SAT.

options.text: Award without any price determination, since there was no competition to compare
options.why: A fair and reasonable price determination is always required.

stem: A 'fair and reasonable' price is:

options.text: Fair to both the Government and the contractor
options.why: It must not be too high for the Government or too low for the contractor to perform.

options.text: The lowest possible price the market will offer
options.why: A price can be too low to be realistic.

options.text: Exactly equal to the IGCE or within five percent
options.why: The IGCE is one benchmark, not the definition.

options.text: Whatever the contractor's catalog says
options.why: Catalog prices still need to be compared with the market.

stem: For a DoW prime contract awarded after 30 June 2026, certified cost or pricing data are required (unless an exception applies) when the contract is expected to exceed:

options.text: $10 million
options.why: The FY2026 NDAA raised DoW's threshold; DoW applies it through the DFARS 215.403-3 class deviation.

options.text: $2.5 million
options.why: $2.5 million is the governmentwide FAR figure and DoW's figure for earlier awards.
That is an outdated figure.
That is the SAT.

stem: Which is an exception to requiring certified cost or pricing data?

options.text: Adequate price competition
options.why: Competition, prices set by law, commercial items and waivers are the main exceptions.

options.text: The contractor is a small business
options.why: Size is not an exception.

options.text: The contract is cost-reimbursement
options.why: Cost-type contracts often require certified data.

options.text: The contract is above $10 million
options.why: That is when data are required, not an exception.

stem: Certified cost or pricing data are never required for:

options.text: Buys at or below the simplified acquisition threshold
options.why: FAR 15.403-2(a) prohibits requiring them at or below the SAT.

options.text: Buys above $10 million for weapon system spare parts
options.why: Large noncompetitive buys often require them.

options.text: Service contracts of any dollar value
options.why: Services are not exempt as such.

options.text: Construction contracts of any dollar value
options.why: Construction is not exempt as such.

stem: A cost is allowable only if it is:

options.text: Reasonable, allocable, consistent with CAS or GAAP and the contract terms, and not disallowed by Part 31
options.why: Those are the factors in FAR 31.201-2.

options.text: Actually incurred, recorded in the contractor's books, and paid before the invoice
options.why: Incurring a cost does not make it allowable.

options.text: Approved by DCAA in a formal audit report and then accepted in writing by the contracting officer for payment
options.why: DCAA advises; the contracting officer decides.

options.text: Shown on an invoice, supported by receipts, and within the contract's ceiling price
options.why: Billing a cost does not make it allowable.

stem: Which cost is unallowable under the cost principles?

options.text: Alcoholic beverages
options.why: FAR 31.205 makes alcohol, entertainment, bad debts and most lobbying unallowable.

options.text: Direct labor on the contract
options.why: Direct labor is normally allowable.

options.text: Materials used on the contract
options.why: Materials are normally allowable.

options.text: Reasonable general and administrative expenses
options.why: Reasonable, allocable G&A is normally allowable.

stem: Cost analysis means:

options.text: Reviewing the separate cost elements and profit in a proposal
options.why: Cost analysis looks inside the price.

options.text: Comparing the prices offered in a competition
options.why: That is price analysis.

options.text: Using dollars per pound to estimate a price
options.why: That is a parametric price analysis technique.

options.text: Finding vendors and comparing their prices during market research
options.why: That is market research.

stem: Cost realism analysis matters most on which contracts?

options.text: Cost-reimbursement contracts
options.why: The Government pays actual costs, so unrealistic estimates lead to overruns.

options.text: Firm-fixed-price commercial contracts
options.why: The contractor carries cost risk; realism is used only in limited cases.

options.text: Micro-purchases
options.why: Micro-purchases need only a reasonable price.

options.text: Sealed bid awards
options.why: Sealed bids are decided on price.

stem: Prenegotiation objectives are:

options.text: The Government's planned positions, set from its analysis before negotiating
options.why: Objectives come from price, cost and technical analysis.

options.text: The contractor's first offer, which the Government then counters
options.why: That is the proposal.

options.text: The final agreed price and terms, recorded in the price negotiation memorandum
options.why: That is the outcome, recorded in the PNM.

options.text: The IGCE, adjusted for the contractor's proposal
options.why: The IGCE is one input, not the objective itself.

stem: Which document records the results of a negotiation?

options.text: The price negotiation memorandum (PNM)
options.why: The PNM documents objectives, positions, the agreement and the reasons.

options.text: The determination and findings
options.why: A D&F approves certain actions; it is not a negotiation record.

options.text: The justification and approval
options.why: A J&A justifies limiting competition.

options.text: The source selection decision document
options.why: That records a competitive award decision.

stem: In negotiation, BATNA means:

options.text: The best alternative to a negotiated agreement
options.why: Knowing your BATNA tells you when to walk away.

options.text: The bid acceptance and tender notice
options.why: No such term.

options.text: The budget allotment for a negotiated award
options.why: Not the meaning.

options.text: The baseline adjusted target amount
options.why: Not the meaning.

stem: Clarifications are:

options.text: Limited exchanges to resolve minor or clerical issues, which never let an offeror revise its proposal
options.why: Under RFO FAR 15.202(a)(2) clarifications may happen at any time after proposals arrive and before award, but they do not open negotiations or allow proposal revisions.

options.text: Negotiations that let every offeror in the competition revise its proposal and its price
options.why: Those are negotiations in the competitive range.

options.text: Debriefings after award that explain the evaluation results
options.why: Debriefings explain the decision after the fact.

options.text: Written protests to the agency about the evaluation
options.why: Protests are disagreements, not exchanges.

stem: The competitive range is made up of:

options.text: The proposals best suited for further negotiation, set when negotiations will be held
options.why: RFO FAR 15.204-1 defines the range as the evaluated proposals best suited for further negotiation; for an efficient competition it may be limited to the most highly rated.

options.text: Every proposal received before the closing date
options.why: Proposals with no reasonable chance can be excluded.

options.text: The three lowest prices, whatever their ratings
options.why: Ratings depend on all factors, not just price.

options.text: Offerors who attended the pre-proposal conference and asked questions in writing
options.why: Attendance does not decide the competitive range.

stem: During negotiations in a competition, which is NOT allowed?

options.text: Telling an offeror another offeror's price
options.why: Revealing competitors' prices or information is prohibited.

options.text: Pointing out significant weaknesses in the offeror's proposal
options.why: That is expected in meaningful negotiations.

options.text: Asking questions about the proposal
options.why: Questions are normal.

options.text: Requesting final proposal revisions
options.why: Final revisions close out negotiations.

stem: A good negotiator makes concessions:

options.text: In exchange for something of value, according to the plan
options.why: Trading concessions keeps the agreement balanced and defensible.

options.text: Early and freely to build trust with the contractor
options.why: Free concessions weaken the Government's position.

options.text: Never, because any concession weakens the position
options.why: Negotiation involves give and take.

options.text: Only through the COR, who knows the requirement
options.why: The contracting officer leads negotiations.

stem: What is the main purpose of planning a negotiation?

options.text: To set your positions on price and terms from your analysis of the offer
options.why: Planning turns your analysis into prenegotiation objectives: the price and terms you aim for and the room you have.

options.text: To fix the final price before the meeting so nothing changes at the table
options.why: Planning sets objectives and a range; the final price comes out of the negotiation itself.

options.text: To give the offeror the Government's objective early so the talks go faster
options.why: Revealing your objective weakens your position; objectives are the Government's internal plan.

options.text: To get the offeror to accept every Government term before talks begin
options.why: Negotiation exists because terms can still move; planning prepares you for that.

stem: The Government and the offeror disagree on delivery dates and price. What should the negotiation aim for?

options.text: Common ground or trade-offs on quantity, price, delivery or quality
options.why: The model describes negotiation as both sides working to find common ground or compromises on quantity, price, delivery, quality and other factors.

options.text: Holding the Government's opening position, since any change is a loss
options.why: Negotiation is give and take; refusing every change is not negotiating.

options.text: Splitting each difference in half so both sides feel treated fairly
options.why: Splitting the difference ignores your analysis; trades should follow your plan.

options.text: Moving to the next offeror as soon as the first one disagrees
options.why: Disagreement is normal; walking away is a fallback, not the first move.

stem: During negotiations an offeror asks about using a different approach from the one the solicitation describes. How should you treat it?

options.text: Consider it if it still meets the solicitation's requirements
options.why: Negotiation can include an alternate approach that stays consistent with the solicitation's requirements.

options.text: Accept it at once if it lowers the price, whatever it changes
options.why: A lower price does not make an approach acceptable; it must still meet the solicitation.

options.text: Treat the question as a reason to drop the offeror from the competition
options.why: Asking about an alternate approach is a normal part of negotiation, not a reason to exclude anyone.

options.text: Allow it only if the other offerors agree to it in writing
options.why: Other offerors do not approve one offeror's approach; the Government decides, and amends the solicitation for everyone if the requirements change.

stem: Which evaluation factor must be part of every source selection?

options.text: Price or cost
options.why: Price or cost must be evaluated in every source selection.

options.text: Past performance
options.why: Past performance is usually but not always evaluated.

options.text: Oral presentations
options.why: Orals are optional.

options.text: Small business participation
options.why: It is evaluated only in some acquisitions.

stem: A tradeoff source selection:

options.text: Allows award to other than the lowest price when the better offer is worth more
options.why: Tradeoffs weigh price against non-price factors.

options.text: Always awards to the lowest price among the acceptable offers
options.why: That is LPTA.

options.text: Does not evaluate technical factors at all, only price and past performance ratings
options.why: Technical factors are central to tradeoffs.

options.text: Cannot be used by DoW for services over $10 million
options.why: Tradeoff is widely used in DoW.

stem: Under lowest price technically acceptable (LPTA):

options.text: Award goes to the lowest priced offer that meets every requirement; no tradeoffs
options.why: LPTA rates proposals acceptable or unacceptable, then picks the lowest acceptable price.

options.text: The best technical proposal wins at any price the Government can afford to pay for it
options.why: That is not LPTA.

options.text: Past performance can never be considered as an acceptability factor
options.why: Past performance can be an acceptability factor.

options.text: Discussions are prohibited once proposals are received
options.why: Discussions are possible in LPTA.

stem: Proposals must be evaluated:

options.text: Only on the factors and subfactors stated in the solicitation
options.why: Using unstated criteria is a leading cause of sustained protests.

options.text: On any factor the SSA decides is relevant
options.why: The SSA is bound by the stated criteria.

options.text: On news stories about the offerors that the team has read
options.why: Outside information must be handled carefully and tied to stated factors.

options.text: Mainly on experience with the incumbent's way of doing the work
options.why: Incumbency is not an evaluation factor.

stem: The source selection authority's decision must:

options.text: Reflect the SSA's own independent judgment and document any tradeoff rationale
options.why: RFO FAR 15.205 requires independent, documented judgment.

options.text: Simply adopt the evaluation board's recommendation and its ratings
options.why: The SSA may use the analysis but must decide independently.

options.text: Be given orally to save time, then summarized in the debriefing
options.why: The decision must be documented.

options.text: Stay secret from the contracting officer and the board until the award is announced
options.why: The contracting officer is the focal point and keeps the file.

stem: Before any award, the contracting officer must make:

options.text: A determination that the prospective contractor is responsible
options.why: No award without a responsibility determination.

options.text: A determination that the contractor is a small business
options.why: Size matters only for set-asides.

options.text: A CPARS evaluation of the contractor's past performance on similar work
options.why: CPARS evaluates performance on existing contracts.

options.text: A DCAA audit of the contractor's accounting system
options.why: Audits are not required for every award.

stem: A contractor is listed as excluded in SAM. Can it receive a new award?

options.text: Generally no, unless the agency head finds a compelling reason
options.why: Excluded contractors may not receive new awards absent a compelling-reason determination.

options.text: Yes, if it has the lowest price and a clean record since
options.why: Price does not overcome an exclusion.

options.text: Yes, if it is a small business and the buy is set aside
options.why: Size does not overcome an exclusion.

options.text: Exclusions matter only for awards above $10 million
options.why: Exclusions apply at every dollar level.

stem: To get a postaward debriefing, an offeror must ask in writing within:

options.text: 3 days after receiving the award notice
options.why: RFO FAR 15.301-1 keys the request window to the award notice.

options.text: 10 days after the contract is awarded
options.why: Ten days is a protest timeline.

options.text: 5 days after the award is announced
options.why: The request window is 3 days.

options.text: 30 days after award, by email
options.why: Far too late.

stem: After a timely request, the agency should hold the postaward debriefing:

options.text: Within 5 days of the request, to the maximum extent practicable
options.why: That is the FAR standard.

options.text: Within 30 days, at a time the offeror chooses
options.why: The target is 5 days.

options.text: Only after any protest has been decided by GAO
options.why: Debriefings come before protests.

options.text: Whenever the source selection authority is free, within the next 60 days
options.why: The 5-day target applies.

stem: In a postaward debriefing, the losing offeror asks to see the winner's technical proposal so it can compare the two. What do you do?

options.text: Decline, and walk through its own evaluation and the winner's overall results
options.why: A debriefing shares overall results, but it must never reveal another offeror's proposal or compare proposals point by point.

options.text: Provide a redacted copy of the winner's technical proposal at the debriefing
options.why: Even redacted, another offeror's proposal is not released in a debriefing.

options.text: Let the offeror read the winner's proposal in your office without making copies
options.why: Showing it at all reveals another offeror's proposal.

options.text: Postpone the debriefing until the offeror files a Freedom of Information Act request
options.why: The debriefing must still be held on time. FOIA is a separate process, and it protects proposals too.

stem: Unsuccessful offerors in the competitive range must get an award notice within:

options.text: 3 days after award
options.why: RFO FAR 15.207-2 requires notice within 3 days.

options.text: 10 days after award
options.why: The requirement is 3 days.

options.text: 30 days after award
options.why: The requirement is 3 days.

options.text: Only if they ask
options.why: Notice is required whether or not they ask.

stem: Where are contract awards reported now that FPDS.gov has been retired?

options.text: In SAM.gov
options.why: Contract award reporting moved into SAM.gov.

options.text: In CPARS
options.why: CPARS holds performance evaluations.

options.text: In PIEE Wide Area WorkFlow
options.why: WAWF holds invoices and receiving reports.

options.text: In GFEBS
options.why: GFEBS is the Army's financial system.

stem: Which item is normally part of a postaward debriefing?

options.text: The winner's and the debriefed offeror's overall price and technical rating
options.why: Debriefings share these overall results.

options.text: A copy of the winner's technical proposal with prices removed
options.why: Other offerors' proposals are not released.

options.text: The names of the evaluators and their individual scoring sheets
options.why: Evaluator identities and individual scores are protected.

options.text: The IGCE line by line, with the Government's negotiation objectives and notes
options.why: The IGCE is not shared.

stem: An offeror excluded from the competitive range wants an explanation before award. It may:

options.text: Ask in writing for a preaward debriefing within 3 days of the notice
options.why: RFO FAR 15.206-2 covers preaward debriefings.

options.text: Never get any explanation until the contract has been awarded
options.why: A preaward debriefing is available on timely request.

options.text: Request a debriefing within 30 days of the exclusion notice
options.why: The window is 3 days.

options.text: Get one only after award, together with the other offerors
options.why: It can be requested before award.

stem: A protest about a problem that is apparent in the solicitation must be filed:

options.text: Before bid opening or the closing time for receipt of proposals
options.why: Offerors cannot wait to see if they win before objecting to the solicitation.

options.text: Within 10 days after award, once the winner is known
options.why: That rule is for other protest grounds.

options.text: Within 5 days after the debriefing, if one is requested
options.why: That rule is for matters learned in a required debriefing.

options.text: Any time during performance, if the problem later causes the offeror harm
options.why: Solicitation challenges must come before closing.

stem: Other GAO protests must generally be filed within how many days after the protester knew or should have known the basis?

options.text: 10 days
options.why: GAO's general timeliness rule is 10 days.

options.text: 5 days
options.why: Five days applies after a required debriefing.

options.text: 30 days
options.why: Thirty days is when the agency report is due.

options.text: 100 days
options.why: One hundred days is GAO's decision deadline.

stem: When a debriefing is required and requested, a protest of matters learned in it can be filed with GAO within:

options.text: 5 days after the debriefing
options.why: This keeps protesters from filing early just to protect their rights.

options.text: 3 days after the debriefing
options.why: Three days is the debriefing request window.

options.text: 10 days after award, no matter when the debriefing is
options.why: The debriefing exception extends the window.

options.text: 30 days after the debriefing
options.why: Too long.

stem: GAO must decide a protest within:

options.text: 100 days
options.why: GAO's statutory deadline is 100 days.

options.text: 35 days
options.why: Thirty-five days is the agency-protest goal.

options.text: 30 days
options.why: Thirty days is the agency report deadline.

options.text: 1 year
options.why: Far longer than the rule.

stem: After award, performance must be suspended for a GAO protest if it was filed within:

options.text: 10 days after award or 5 days after a required debriefing, if later
options.why: That is the automatic stay rule under CICA.

options.text: 30 days after award or 10 days after any debriefing
options.why: The stay window is shorter.

options.text: Any time before the contract is completed, if GAO agrees that the issue is urgent
options.why: Only timely protests trigger the stay.

options.text: 3 days after award or after the award notice is received
options.why: The window is 10 days, or 5 after a required debriefing.

stem: Who can override the automatic stay of a GAO protest?

options.text: The head of the contracting activity, with a written finding
options.why: Overrides are reserved to the HCA level and must be justified.

options.text: The contracting officer, after telling GAO and the protester in writing
options.why: The contracting officer cannot override on their own.

options.text: The COR, when the customer's mission is at risk
options.why: The COR has no such authority.

options.text: The awardee, by posting a performance bond
options.why: Contractors cannot override stays.

stem: For DoW, GAO hears protests of task or delivery orders valued above what amount (or orders that increase the contract's scope, period or maximum value)?

options.text: $35 million
options.why: The FY2025 NDAA raised DoW's order-protest floor from $25 million to $35 million.

options.text: $10 million
options.why: $10 million is the civilian agency figure.

options.text: $25 million
options.why: That was DoW's figure before the FY2025 NDAA.

options.text: $7.5 million
options.why: $7.5 million is a fair-opportunity procedures tier, not a protest floor.
